# Chapter 5: M- and Z-Estimators {#sec-m-z-estimators}

This chapter develops a reusable route from an empirical optimization problem or estimating equation to consistency, an asymptotic-linear expansion, and a rate of convergence. Chapter 25 repeatedly uses this route after replacing a fixed finite-dimensional nuisance parameter by an estimated function.

::: {.callout-tip title="Why this chapter is here"}

- **Prerequisites:** [stochastic order and Slutsky's lemma](chapter-2.qmd#sec-stochastic-order), the [empirical measure](glossary.qmd#glossary-empirical-measure), and basic differentiation.
- **Purpose:** separate the global argument that places an estimator near the truth from the local argument that determines its first-order distribution.
- **Chapter 25 payoff:** [efficient score equations](chapter-25.qmd#sec-efficient-score-equations), [general estimating equations](chapter-25.qmd#sec-general-estimating-equations), one-step corrections, and nuisance-rate arguments all reuse the structure developed here.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Companion reading"}

For a parallel treatment of M- and Z-estimators, their asymptotic distributions, and one-step estimation, see [@bailie2021, §§1.2, 4.3, 7.2, and 8.1].

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Reading guide" collapse="true"}

The route to Chapter 25 uses selected parts of the source chapter:

- [§5.1](#sec-5-1) distinguishes maximization from root finding.
- [§5.2](#sec-5-2) gives the global consistency step.
- [§5.3](#sec-5-3) gives the local Z-estimator expansion.
- [§5.4](#sec-5-4) shows how an estimated nuisance parameter creates a drift term.
- [§5.7](#sec-5-7) replaces exact root finding by one Newton step.
- [§5.8](#sec-5-8) balances curvature against empirical-process oscillation and then allows a nuisance parameter.

Within the selected sections, Examples 5.26–5.27 and 5.32–5.33 are compressed to their reusable mechanisms. The following material is deliberately omitted from the route:

- the one-dimensional root lemma, median, Wald-consistency theorem, and its Cauchy/current-status applications (Lemma 5.10, Example 5.11, Theorem 5.14, and Examples 5.16–5.17);
- the M-estimator expansion and applications not reused later (Theorem 5.23 and Examples 5.24–5.25 and 5.28–5.29);
- §§5.5–5.6 on maximum-likelihood and classical smoothness conditions;
- Addendum 5.46 and Examples 5.50–5.51, which refine the one-step construction without changing its mechanism; and
- Corollary 5.53, Example 5.54, Theorem 5.56, and Corollary 5.58 on specialized rates and general argmax convergence.

:::

| Does the empirical optimizer or root approach the population one? | [Theorems 5.7](#theorem-5-7) and [5.9](#theorem-5-9) | Consistency before local expansion |

## 5.1 Introduction {#sec-5-1}

Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be identically distributed with law $P$. Write

$$
\mathbb P_nf=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nf(X_i),
\qquad
\mathbb G_nf=\sqrt n(\mathbb P_n-P)f.
$$

The source studies two related ways to define an estimator.

::: {.callout-note title="Definitions"}

An [M-estimator](glossary.qmd#glossary-m-estimator) maximizes, or nearly maximizes, a criterion

$$
M_n(\theta)=\mathbb P_nm_\theta.
\tag{5.1}
$$

A [Z-estimator](glossary.qmd#glossary-z-estimator) solves, or nearly solves, a vector equation

$$
\Psi_n(\theta)=\mathbb P_n\psi_\theta=0.
\tag{5.2}
$$

The letter Z refers to a zero. A differentiable M-criterion may generate a Z-equation by differentiation, but an estimating equation need not be the derivative of any objective function.

:::

Near maximizers and approximate roots are part of the theory, not merely numerical compromises. The relevant tolerance depends on the conclusion:

- consistency usually requires only an $o_P(1)$ criterion gap or root residual;
- a root-$n$ expansion requires a root residual of order $o_P(n^{-1/2})$;
- a rate theorem requires the optimization error to be no larger than the deterministic criterion drop at that rate.

Maximum likelihood is an M-procedure with $m_\theta=\log p_\theta$ and, when differentiable, a Z-procedure with $\psi_\theta=\dot\ell_\theta$. Location estimates supply less smooth examples: the mean solves a linear equation, while a median is a near zero of a sign equation. The distinction matters because a maximizer may exist when no useful derivative does, and a discontinuous estimating function may still yield a regular estimator.

::: {.callout-tip title="The progression used later"}

The chapter deliberately separates two jobs:

1. a **global** criterion argument proves $\widehat\theta_n\overset P\to\theta_0$;
2. a **local** expansion around $\theta_0$ identifies $\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0)$.

Chapter 25 follows the same division. Nuisance estimation and empirical-process conditions enter the local step only after consistency has placed the estimator in the relevant neighborhood.

:::

## 5.2 Consistency {#sec-5-2}

Suppose $M_n$ approaches a deterministic population criterion $M$. Pointwise convergence is not enough: because $\widehat\theta_n$ is selected from the entire random function, the criterion must be controlled uniformly, and the population optimum must be separated from competing parameter values.

::: {.callout-note title="Theorem"}
### Theorem 5.7: consistency of near maximizers {#theorem-5-7}

Let $M_n$ be random functions on a metric space $\Theta$, and let $M$ be a fixed function. Suppose

$$
\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}|M_n(\theta)-M(\theta)|
\overset P\longrightarrow0,
$$

and, for every $\varepsilon>0$,

$$
\sup_{\theta:d(\theta,\theta_0)\geq\varepsilon}M(\theta)
<M(\theta_0).
\tag{5.8}
$$

If

$$
M_n(\widehat\theta_n)\geq M_n(\theta_0)-o_P(1),
$$

then $\widehat\theta_n\overset P\to\theta_0$.

:::

**Proof roadmap.** Uniform convergence transfers near maximization from $M_n$ to $M$; the separation condition then turns a small population criterion gap into consistency.

<details>
<summary>Complete proof</summary>

The near-maximization property and uniform convergence give

$$
M_n(\widehat\theta_n)
\geq M_n(\theta_0)-o_P(1)
=M(\theta_0)-o_P(1).
$$

Consequently,

$$
\begin{aligned}
M(\theta_0)-M(\widehat\theta_n)
&\leq M_n(\widehat\theta_n)-M(\widehat\theta_n)+o_P(1)\\
&\leq \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}|M_n(\theta)-M(\theta)|+o_P(1)
\overset P\longrightarrow0.
\end{aligned}
$$

Fix $\varepsilon>0$. By the separation assumption there is an $\eta>0$ such that

$$
M(\theta)\leq M(\theta_0)-\eta
\qquad\text{whenever }d(\theta,\theta_0)\geq\varepsilon.
$$

Hence

$$
\{d(\widehat\theta_n,\theta_0)\geq\varepsilon\}
\subseteq
\{M(\theta_0)-M(\widehat\theta_n)\geq\eta\}.
$$

The probability of the event on the right tends to zero by the preceding convergence. This holds for every $\varepsilon>0$, proving consistency.

</details>

For empirical criteria $M_n(\theta)=\mathbb P_nm_\theta$, the stochastic assumption is a uniform law of large numbers: the class $\{m_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}$ must be Glivenko--Cantelli. [Chapter 19](chapter-19.qmd#glivenko-cantelli-classes) supplies systematic ways to verify that condition.

The same logic applies to roots after turning distance from zero into a criterion.

::: {.callout-note title="Theorem"}
### Theorem 5.9: consistency of approximate roots {#theorem-5-9}

Let $\Psi_n$ be random vector-valued functions and let $\Psi$ be fixed. Suppose

$$
\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\|\Psi_n(\theta)-\Psi(\theta)\|
\overset P\longrightarrow0,
$$

and, for every $\varepsilon>0$,

$$
\inf_{\theta:d(\theta,\theta_0)\geq\varepsilon}
\|\Psi(\theta)\|>0=\|\Psi(\theta_0)\|.
$$

If $\Psi_n(\widehat\theta_n)=o_P(1)$, then $\widehat\theta_n\overset P\to\theta_0$.

:::

**Proof roadmap.** Turn distance from zero into the criterion $-\|\Psi_n\|$, verify the hypotheses of Theorem 5.7 by the reverse triangle inequality, and invoke that theorem.

<details>
<summary>Complete proof</summary>

Set

$$
M_n(\theta)=-\|\Psi_n(\theta)\|,
\qquad
M(\theta)=-\|\Psi(\theta)\|.
$$

The reverse triangle inequality gives

$$
\sup_\theta|M_n(\theta)-M(\theta)|
\leq
\sup_\theta\|\Psi_n(\theta)-\Psi(\theta)\|
\overset P\longrightarrow0.
$$

The deterministic condition in the theorem says exactly that $\theta_0$ is a well-separated maximizer of $M$. Moreover,

$$
M_n(\widehat\theta_n)
=-\|\Psi_n(\widehat\theta_n)\|
=-o_P(1)
\geq M_n(\theta_0)-o_P(1),
$$

because $\Psi_n(\theta_0)=\Psi(\theta_0)+o_P(1)=o_P(1)$. Theorem 5.7 now yields $\widehat\theta_n\overset P\to\theta_0$.

</details>

::: {.callout-warning title="Consistency does not provide the distribution"}

Uniform convergence controls the criterion on a large parameter set. The asymptotic distribution instead depends on increasingly small neighborhoods of $\theta_0$. A proof should not blur these two scales: establish consistency first, then invoke the local stochastic expansion below.

:::

## 5.3 Asymptotic Normality {#sec-5-3}

Suppose $P\psi_{\theta_0}=0$ and $\widehat\theta_n$ approximately solves $\mathbb P_n\psi_\theta=0$. A formal Taylor expansion suggests

$$
0
\approx
\mathbb P_n\psi_{\theta_0}
+V_{\theta_0}(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0),
\qquad
V_{\theta_0}
=\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}P\psi_\theta\right|_{\theta=\theta_0}.
$$

Solving the linear equation gives the prototype expansion

$$
\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0)
\approx
-V_{\theta_0}^{-1}\mathbb G_n\psi_{\theta_0}.
$$

The derivative is taken on the **population** equation. The randomness is isolated in the empirical average at the truth. The resulting covariance has the [sandwich form](glossary.qmd#glossary-sandwich)

$$
V_{\theta_0}^{-1}
\{P\psi_{\theta_0}\psi_{\theta_0}^T\}
(V_{\theta_0}^{-1})^T.
$$

The next theorem makes the expansion rigorous without requiring two pointwise derivatives of $\theta\mapsto\psi_\theta(x)$.

::: {.callout-note title="Theorem"}
### Theorem 5.21: asymptotic linearity of Z-estimators {#theorem-5-21}

For each $\theta$ in an open subset of Euclidean space, let $x\mapsto\psi_\theta(x)$ be a measurable vector-valued function. Suppose that, for $\theta_1,\theta_2$ in a neighborhood of $\theta_0$,

$$
\|\psi_{\theta_1}(x)-\psi_{\theta_2}(x)\|
\leq \dot\psi(x)\|\theta_1-\theta_2\|,
$$

for a measurable $\dot\psi$ with $P\dot\psi^2<\infty$. Assume $P\|\psi_{\theta_0}\|^2<\infty$ and that $\theta\mapsto P\psi_\theta$ is differentiable at its zero $\theta_0$, with nonsingular derivative matrix $V_{\theta_0}$.

If

$$
\mathbb P_n\psi_{\widehat\theta_n}=o_P(n^{-1/2})
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\widehat\theta_n\overset P\longrightarrow\theta_0,
$$

then

$$
\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0)
=-V_{\theta_0}^{-1}\mathbb G_n\psi_{\theta_0}+o_P(1).
\tag{5.20}
$$

In particular, the limit is mean-zero normal with covariance

$$
V_{\theta_0}^{-1}
P\psi_{\theta_0}\psi_{\theta_0}^T
(V_{\theta_0}^{-1})^T.
$$

:::

**Proof roadmap.** Stochastic equicontinuity replaces the estimating function at the random root by its value at $\theta_0$; differentiability linearizes the population equation; nonsingularity then yields the rate and the asymptotic expansion.

<details>
<summary>Complete proof</summary>

The first task is to replace the estimating function at $\widehat\theta_n$ by the one at $\theta_0$ inside the empirical process:

$$
\mathbb G_n(\psi_{\widehat\theta_n}-\psi_{\theta_0})=o_P(1).
\tag{5.22}
$$

For a nonrandom sequence $\theta_n\to\theta_0$, the left side has mean zero and variance bounded by

$$
P\|\psi_{\theta_n}-\psi_{\theta_0}\|^2
\leq P\dot\psi^2\|\theta_n-\theta_0\|^2\longrightarrow0.
$$

For the random sequence $\widehat\theta_n$, the same conclusion is a stochastic-equicontinuity statement. Under the displayed Lipschitz envelope the class is Donsker; [Lemma 19.24](chapter-19.qmd#lemma-19.24) and consistency give (5.22).

Because $P\psi_{\theta_0}=0$ and $\mathbb P_n\psi_{\widehat\theta_n}=o_P(n^{-1/2})$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb G_n\psi_{\theta_0}
&=\mathbb G_n\psi_{\widehat\theta_n}+o_P(1)\\
&=\sqrt n\{\mathbb P_n\psi_{\widehat\theta_n}-P\psi_{\widehat\theta_n}\}+o_P(1)\\
&=-\sqrt nP\psi_{\widehat\theta_n}+o_P(1).
\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiability of the population map at $\theta_0$ gives

$$
P\psi_{\widehat\theta_n}
=V_{\theta_0}(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0)
+o_P(\|\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0\|).
$$

Combining the last two displays,

$$
\mathbb G_n\psi_{\theta_0}
+\sqrt nV_{\theta_0}(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0)
=o_P(1)+o_P\{\sqrt n\|\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0\|\}.
$$

The central limit theorem gives $\mathbb G_n\psi_{\theta_0}=O_P(1)$. Since $V_{\theta_0}$ is nonsingular, the last display implies

$$
\sqrt n\|\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0\|
\leq O_P(1)+o_P\{\sqrt n\|\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0\|\},
$$

and hence $\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0)=O_P(1)$. Substitute this rate back into the preceding expansion and multiply by $-V_{\theta_0}^{-1}$ to obtain (5.20). The multivariate central limit theorem gives the stated normal covariance.

</details>

::: {.callout-tip title="Example 5.26: exponential frailty"}

In the source's paired-survival model, an unobserved frailty $Z$ makes $X$ and $Y$ conditionally exponential with rates $Z$ and $\theta Z$. A conditionally motivated score is biased, so the source corrects it by subtracting its conditional expectation given the sufficient statistic $X+\theta Y$. The resulting bounded estimating function has a unique consistent root and Theorem 5.21 gives asymptotic normality.

The estimator is not efficient. This is the early version of a recurring message: a valid mean-zero equation need not use all available information. The model returns in [Example 25.9](chapter-25.qmd#example-25-9) and [§25.11.2](chapter-25.qmd#sec-25-11-exponential-frailty), where a least-favorable path identifies the efficient score.

:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Example 5.27: nonlinear least squares"}

For $Y=f_{\theta_0}(X)+\varepsilon$ with $E(\varepsilon\mid X)=0$, nonlinear least squares uses

$$
m_\theta(x,y)=-\{y-f_\theta(x)\}^2.
$$

Its local expansion has a first-order summand proportional to

$$
\{P\dot f_{\theta_0}\dot f_{\theta_0}^T\}^{-1}
\dot f_{\theta_0}(X)\varepsilon.
$$

This is the finite-dimensional predecessor of the regression influence functions in [Example 25.28](chapter-25.qmd#example-25-28) and [Example 25.66](chapter-25.qmd#example-25-66). Chapter 25 asks which residual weight gives the smallest variance when the conditional variance is unknown.

:::

## 5.4* Estimated Parameters {#sec-5-4}

Now let the estimating function depend on a nuisance parameter $\eta$ and suppose $\widehat\eta_n$ is substituted into the equation. Even if $\widehat\eta_n\to\eta_0$, its effect may remain visible after multiplication by $\sqrt n$.

::: {.callout-note title="Theorem"}
### Theorem 5.31: estimated nuisance parameters {#theorem-5-31}

For $\theta$ in an open subset of $\mathbb R^k$ and $\eta$ in a metric space, let $\psi_{\theta,\eta}$ be $\mathbb R^k$-valued. Suppose, locally around $(\theta_0,\eta_0)$,

- the class $\{\psi_{\theta,\eta}:\|\theta-\theta_0\|<\delta, d(\eta,\eta_0)<\delta\}$ is Donsker;
- $P\|\psi_{\theta,\eta}-\psi_{\theta_0,\eta_0}\|^2\to0$ as $(\theta,\eta)\to(\theta_0,\eta_0)$;
- $P\psi_{\theta_0,\eta_0}=0$;
- the maps $\theta\mapsto P\psi_{\theta,\eta}$ are differentiable at $\theta_0$, uniformly for nearby $\eta$, with nonsingular derivative matrices $V_{\theta_0,\eta}\to V_{\theta_0,\eta_0}$.

If

$$
\sqrt n\,\mathbb P_n\psi_{\widehat\theta_n,\widehat\eta_n}=o_P(1),
\qquad
(\widehat\theta_n,\widehat\eta_n)\overset P\longrightarrow(\theta_0,\eta_0),
$$

then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0)
={}&-V_{\theta_0,\eta_0}^{-1}
\sqrt nP\psi_{\theta_0,\widehat\eta_n}
-V_{\theta_0,\eta_0}^{-1}\mathbb G_n\psi_{\theta_0,\eta_0}\\
&+o_P\!\left(1+\sqrt n\|P\psi_{\theta_0,\widehat\eta_n}\|\right).
\tag{5.31}
\end{aligned}
$$

:::

**Proof roadmap.** Separate the empirical fluctuation from the population equation, keep the nuisance-induced population drift, linearize only in $\theta$, and solve the resulting equation.

<details>
<summary>Derivation in these notes of (5.31)</summary>

The Donsker and $L_2(P)$ continuity assumptions give

$$
\mathbb G_n
\{\psi_{\widehat\theta_n,\widehat\eta_n}
-\psi_{\theta_0,\eta_0}\}=o_P(1).
$$

The approximate estimating equation can therefore be written

$$
0
=\mathbb G_n\psi_{\theta_0,\eta_0}
+\sqrt nP\psi_{\widehat\theta_n,\widehat\eta_n}
+o_P(1).
$$

Uniform differentiability in $\theta$ gives

$$
P\psi_{\widehat\theta_n,\widehat\eta_n}
=P\psi_{\theta_0,\widehat\eta_n}
+V_{\theta_0,\widehat\eta_n}(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0)
+o_P(\|\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0\|).
$$

As in the proof of Theorem 5.21, nonsingularity first yields the rate

$$
\sqrt n\|\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0\|
=O_P\!\left(1+\sqrt n\|P\psi_{\theta_0,\widehat\eta_n}\|\right).
$$

Substituting that rate into the expansion, replacing $V_{\theta_0,\widehat\eta_n}$ by its probability limit, and solving the linear equation yields (5.31).

</details>

The first term in (5.31),

$$
\sqrt nP\psi_{\theta_0,\widehat\eta_n},
$$

is the nuisance **drift**. Mere consistency of $\widehat\eta_n$ does not make it negligible at the root-$n$ scale. Chapter 25 calls the required control a [no-bias condition](glossary.qmd#glossary-no-bias); in modern moment terminology, a vanishing nuisance derivative is [Neyman orthogonality](glossary.qmd#glossary-neyman-orthogonality). The source result comes first: the drift must be calculated and controlled.

::: {.callout-tip title="Example 5.32: symmetric location"}

Suppose $P$ is symmetric about $\theta_0$ and $\psi$ is odd. In the scale-adjusted equation

$$
\mathbb P_n\psi\!\left(\frac{X-\theta}{\widehat\sigma_n}\right)=0,
$$

symmetry gives

$$
P\psi\!\left(\frac{X-\theta_0}{\sigma}\right)=0
$$

for every $\sigma$, not only at $\sigma_0$. The nuisance drift is therefore exactly zero for any consistent scale estimate. This is an early adaptivity argument: [Example 25.27](chapter-25.qmd#example-25-27) explains it as orthogonality of odd target scores and even nuisance scores, and [§25.8.1](chapter-25.qmd#sec-25-8-symmetric-location) constructs an efficient estimator when the score itself is unknown.

:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Example 5.33: adaptive weights"}

In robust regression, the score may contain estimated weight functions. If the population equation remains zero for every admissible limiting weight, their first-order drift vanishes even when the weights are learned from the data. The weights can then be chosen to improve robustness or asymptotic variance.

This is the finite-dimensional precursor of [general estimating equations in §25.9](chapter-25.qmd#sec-general-estimating-equations): validity can hold across a family of weights, while efficiency selects the optimal member. Modern cross-fitting changes how the empirical-process term is controlled, not the need to control the population drift.

:::

## 5.7* One-Step Estimators {#sec-5-7}

An exact Z-root may be difficult to find or may have unwanted distant roots. The one-step method starts from a root-$n$ consistent preliminary estimator $\widetilde\theta_n$ and solves a linear approximation to $\Psi_n(\theta)=0$ once.

Given nonsingular matrices $\dot\Psi_{n,0}\overset P\to\dot\Psi_0$, define

$$
\widehat\theta_n
=\widetilde\theta_n
-\dot\Psi_{n,0}^{-1}\Psi_n(\widetilde\theta_n).
\tag{5.43}
$$

The source calls $\widetilde\theta_n$ root-$n$ consistent when $\sqrt n(\widetilde\theta_n-\theta_0)$ is uniformly tight. Assume that, for every fixed $M<\infty$,

$$
\sup_{\sqrt n\|\theta-\theta_0\|<M}
\left\|
\sqrt n\{\Psi_n(\theta)-\Psi_n(\theta_0)\}
-\dot\Psi_0\sqrt n(\theta-\theta_0)
\right\|
\overset P\longrightarrow0.
\tag{5.44}
$$

This is a local linearization of the random estimating equation; it does not require a pointwise derivative $\dot\Psi_n$ to exist.

::: {.callout-note title="Theorem"}
### Theorem 5.45: one-step estimation {#theorem-5-45}

Suppose $\sqrt n\Psi_n(\theta_0)\rightsquigarrow Z$ and (5.44) holds. For any root-$n$ consistent $\widetilde\theta_n$ and any $\dot\Psi_{n,0}\overset P\to\dot\Psi_0$, the estimator in (5.43) satisfies

$$
\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0)
=-\dot\Psi_0^{-1}\sqrt n\Psi_n(\theta_0)+o_P(1).
\tag{5.45}
$$

:::

**Proof roadmap.** Expand the empirical equation once around the preliminary estimator. The Newton correction cancels its root-$n$ error, while consistency of the derivative estimate and the local remainder make every replacement negligible.

<details>
<summary>Complete proof</summary>

Multiply the definition of $\widehat\theta_n$ by $\dot\Psi_{n,0}\sqrt n$ and add and subtract $\Psi_n(\theta_0)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\dot\Psi_{n,0}\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0)
={}&\dot\Psi_{n,0}\sqrt n(\widetilde\theta_n-\theta_0)\\
&-\sqrt n\{\Psi_n(\widetilde\theta_n)-\Psi_n(\theta_0)\}
-\sqrt n\Psi_n(\theta_0).
\end{aligned}
$$

Root-$n$ consistency places $\widetilde\theta_n$ in a bounded local neighborhood with arbitrarily high probability. Condition (5.44) therefore gives

$$
\sqrt n\{\Psi_n(\widetilde\theta_n)-\Psi_n(\theta_0)\}
=\dot\Psi_0\sqrt n(\widetilde\theta_n-\theta_0)+o_P(1).
$$

Hence

$$
\dot\Psi_{n,0}\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0)
=(\dot\Psi_{n,0}-\dot\Psi_0)
\sqrt n(\widetilde\theta_n-\theta_0)
-\sqrt n\Psi_n(\theta_0)+o_P(1).
$$

The first term is $o_P(1)$ because the matrix difference converges to zero in probability and the preliminary error is tight. Since $\dot\Psi_{n,0}^{-1}\overset P\to\dot\Psi_0^{-1}$, Slutsky's lemma yields (5.45).

</details>

The preliminary estimator supplies localization; the one-step correction supplies the first-order distribution. Further Newton iterations may improve numerical accuracy, but they do not improve the first-order limit in (5.45).

::: {.callout-tip title="From Newton correction to influence-function correction"}

When $\Psi_n$ is an efficient score equation, $-\dot\Psi_0^{-1}\Psi_n(\widetilde\theta_n)$ is an empirical average of an estimated efficient influence function. [Section 25.8](chapter-25.qmd#sec-25-8-one-step) rewrites the same operation as a bias correction to a plug-in estimator. Double/debiased machine learning retains this one-step architecture while using cross-fitting and target-specific remainder bounds to accommodate flexible nuisance fits.

:::

### Discretized one-step estimation

Condition (5.44) is uniform over random local arguments. The source's discretization device replaces it by a condition only along deterministic local sequences. For every nonrandom $\theta_n=\theta_0+O(n^{-1/2})$, assume

$$
\left\|
\sqrt n\{\Psi_n(\theta_n)-\Psi_n(\theta_0)\}
-\dot\Psi_0\sqrt n(\theta_n-\theta_0)
\right\|
\overset P\longrightarrow0.
\tag{5.47}
$$

Round a preliminary estimator to a grid with mesh $n^{-1/2}$, for example $n^{-1/2}\mathbb Z^k$. Rounding changes each coordinate by at most order $n^{-1/2}$, so root-$n$ consistency is retained.

::: {.callout-note title="Theorem"}
### Theorem 5.48: discretized one-step estimation {#theorem-5-48}

Suppose $\sqrt n\Psi_n(\theta_0)\rightsquigarrow Z$ and (5.47) holds. If $\widetilde\theta_n$ is root-$n$ consistent and discretized, and $\dot\Psi_{n,0}\overset P\to\dot\Psi_0$, then its one-step update satisfies

$$
\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0)
=-\dot\Psi_0^{-1}\sqrt n\Psi_n(\theta_0)+o_P(1).
$$

:::

::: {.callout-important title="Addendum 5.49"}

Let $\Psi_n(\theta)=\mathbb P_n\psi_\theta$ for a sample from $p_{\theta_0}$, and suppose the model is differentiable in quadratic mean at $\theta_0$. Then (5.47) holds with

$$
\dot\Psi_0
=-P_{\theta_0}\psi_{\theta_0}\dot\ell_{\theta_0}^T,
$$

provided

$$
\int
\left[
\psi_\theta\sqrt{p_\theta}
-\psi_{\theta_0}\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}
\right]^2d\mu
\longrightarrow0
\qquad\text{as }\theta\to\theta_0.
\tag{5.49}
$$

:::

**Proof roadmap.** Discretize the root-$n$ neighborhood into finitely many possible preliminary values. Pointwise control along every deterministic local sequence then becomes uniform over the discretized estimator, after which Theorem 5.45 applies.

<details>
<summary>Complete proof of the discretization step</summary>

Fix $M$. On the event $\sqrt n\|\widetilde\theta_n-\theta_0\|\leq M$, a grid with mesh $n^{-1/2}$ contains only a bounded number of possible values for $\widetilde\theta_n$ inside that local ball. Call this finite set $S_n$.

For the remainder

$$
R_n(\theta)
=\sqrt n\{\Psi_n(\theta)-\Psi_n(\theta_0)\}
-\dot\Psi_0\sqrt n(\theta-\theta_0),
$$

and any $\varepsilon>0$,

$$
P\{\|R_n(\widetilde\theta_n)\|>\varepsilon\}
\leq
P\{\sqrt n\|\widetilde\theta_n-\theta_0\|>M\}
+\sum_{\theta\in S_n}P\{\|R_n(\theta)\|>\varepsilon\}.
$$

The first term is made small by root-$n$ consistency. The set $S_n$ has uniformly bounded cardinality, and every choice of one point from each $S_n$ is a deterministic sequence $\theta_n=\theta_0+O(n^{-1/2})$. Condition (5.47) therefore makes the largest probability in the sum tend to zero. The proof of Theorem 5.45 now applies.

Addendum 5.49 shows why the device was important in the source: quadratic-mean differentiability and an $L_2$ continuity condition suffice for the deterministic-sequence expansion, even when uniform stochastic differentiability is inconvenient to prove.

</details>

## 5.8* Rates of Convergence {#sec-5-8}

For an M-estimator, the rate is determined by a competition:

- the population criterion falls as $\theta$ moves away from $\theta_0$;
- the empirical process fluctuates over the same neighborhood.

Let $d$ be a metric on $\Theta$. The next theorem represents population curvature by an exponent $\alpha$ and local stochastic oscillation by an exponent $\beta$.

::: {.callout-note title="Theorem"}
### Theorem 5.52: rate of convergence {#theorem-5-52}

Assume that, for constants $C>0$ and $\alpha>\beta$, every $n$, and all sufficiently small $\delta>0$,

$$
\sup_{\delta/2\leq d(\theta,\theta_0)<\delta}
P(m_\theta-m_{\theta_0})
\leq-C\delta^\alpha,
$$

and

$$
E^*\sup_{d(\theta,\theta_0)<\delta}
|\mathbb G_n(m_\theta-m_{\theta_0})|
\leq C\delta^\beta.
$$

If $\widehat\theta_n\to\theta_0$ in outer probability and

$$
\mathbb P_nm_{\widehat\theta_n}
\geq
\mathbb P_nm_{\theta_0}
-O_P\!\left(n^{\alpha/(2\beta-2\alpha)}\right),
$$

then

$$
n^{1/(2\alpha-2\beta)}d(\widehat\theta_n,\theta_0)
=O_P^*(1).
$$

:::

**Proof roadmap.** Partition the parameter space into dyadic shells at the candidate rate. On each shell, deterministic curvature must dominate both the empirical fluctuation and the permitted optimization error; summing the shell probabilities gives tightness at that rate.

<details>
<summary>Complete proof</summary>

Set

$$
r_n=n^{1/(2\alpha-2\beta)}.
$$

Then $r_n^{\alpha-\beta}=\sqrt n$, and the allowed criterion error is $O_P(r_n^{-\alpha})$. Write it as a nonnegative random variable $R_n=O_P(r_n^{-\alpha})$.

Partition the parameter space away from $\theta_0$ into shells

$$
S_{j,n}
=\left\{\theta:2^{j-1}<r_nd(\theta,\theta_0)\leq2^j\right\},
\qquad j\in\mathbb Z.
$$

If $r_nd(\widehat\theta_n,\theta_0)>2^M$, then $\widehat\theta_n$ belongs to a shell $S_{j,n}$ with $j\geq M$. On that shell, near maximization implies

$$
\sup_{\theta\in S_{j,n}}
\mathbb P_n(m_\theta-m_{\theta_0})\geq-R_n.
$$

Fix a small $\varepsilon>0$ on which the theorem's bounds hold and a constant $K$. Up to the event $\{2d(\widehat\theta_n,\theta_0)\geq\varepsilon\}$ and the event $\{r_n^\alpha R_n\geq K\}$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
P^*\{r_nd(\widehat\theta_n,\theta_0)>2^M\}
\leq
\sum_{\substack{j\geq M\\2^j\leq\varepsilon r_n}}
P^*\left\{
\sup_{\theta\in S_{j,n}}
\mathbb P_n(m_\theta-m_{\theta_0})
\geq-\frac{K}{r_n^\alpha}
\right\}
+o(1).
\end{aligned}
$$

Consistency makes the first excluded event vanish, and $R_n=O_P(r_n^{-\alpha})$ makes the second uniformly small for large $K$. For $\theta\in S_{j,n}$, the deterministic condition gives

$$
P(m_\theta-m_{\theta_0})
\leq-C\frac{2^{(j-1)\alpha}}{r_n^\alpha}.
$$

Choose $M$ so large that $K\leq \frac12C2^{(M-1)\alpha}$. Then the event inside the sum requires

$$
\sup_{\theta\in S_{j,n}}
|\mathbb G_n(m_\theta-m_{\theta_0})|
\geq
\frac{C\sqrt n\,2^{(j-1)\alpha}}{2r_n^\alpha}.
$$

By Markov's inequality and the oscillation bound on the ball of radius $2^j/r_n$, its probability is at most a constant multiple of

$$
\frac{(2^j/r_n)^\beta}
{\sqrt n\,2^{(j-1)\alpha}/r_n^\alpha}
=C'2^{-j(\alpha-\beta)},
$$

because $r_n^{\alpha-\beta}=\sqrt n$. Therefore

$$
\sum_{j\geq M}C'2^{-j(\alpha-\beta)}\longrightarrow0
\qquad\text{as }M\to\infty,
$$

since $\alpha>\beta$. Thus $r_nd(\widehat\theta_n,\theta_0)=O_P^*(1)$.

</details>

In a regular Euclidean problem, a nonsingular quadratic population expansion gives $\alpha=2$, while a Lipschitz empirical criterion typically gives $\beta=1$. The theorem then yields $r_n=\sqrt n$. If $\alpha=2$ and $\beta=1/2$, the balance gives $r_n=n^{1/3}$, the familiar cube-root rate.

### 5.8.1 Nuisance Parameters {#sec-5-8-1}

The source explicitly introduces the next theorem because Chapter 25 needs a rate result when the criterion contains an estimated smoothing or nuisance parameter.

Let $m_{\theta,\eta}$ be indexed by $(\theta,\eta)\in\Theta_n\times H_n$. The source allows problem-specific discrepancy functions $d_\eta(\theta,\theta_0)$ and $d(\eta,\eta_0)$; they need not arise from metrics.

::: {.callout-note title="Theorem"}
### Theorem 5.55: rate with a nuisance parameter {#theorem-5-55}

Suppose there are functions

$$
e_n:\Theta_n\times H_n\to\mathbb R,
\qquad
\phi_n:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R,
$$

such that $\delta\mapsto\phi_n(\delta)/\delta^\beta$ is decreasing for some $\beta<2$. Assume, for every $(\theta,\eta)\in\Theta_n\times H_n$ and every $\delta>0$,

$$
P(m_{\theta,\eta}-m_{\theta_0,\eta})+e_n(\theta,\eta)
\leq
-d_\eta^2(\theta,\theta_0)+d^2(\eta,\eta_0),
\tag{5.55a}
$$

and

$$
E^*\!
\sup_{\substack{d_\eta(\theta,\theta_0)<\delta\\
(\theta,\eta)\in\Theta_n\times H_n}}
\left|
\mathbb G_n(m_{\theta,\eta}-m_{\theta_0,\eta})
-\sqrt n e_n(\theta,\eta)
\right|
\leq\phi_n(\delta).
\tag{5.55b}
$$

Let $\delta_n>0$ satisfy

$$
\phi_n(\delta_n)\leq\sqrt n\,\delta_n^2.
$$

If

$$
P(\widehat\theta_n\in\Theta_n,\widehat\eta_n\in H_n)\to1
$$

and

$$
\mathbb P_nm_{\widehat\theta_n,\widehat\eta_n}
\geq
\mathbb P_nm_{\theta_0,\widehat\eta_n}
-O_P(\delta_n^2),
$$

then

$$
d_{\widehat\eta_n}(\widehat\theta_n,\theta_0)
=O_P^*\{\delta_n+d(\widehat\eta_n,\eta_0)\}.
$$

:::

**Proof roadmap.** Peel jointly over target error and nuisance discrepancy. Curvature controls target movement beyond the nuisance floor; the empirical modulus controls each shell; a geometric-series bound yields the intrinsic rate plus nuisance error.

<details>
<summary>Complete proof</summary>

First suppose the empirical criterion is maximized without a tolerance term. For $j\in\mathbb Z$ and $M>0$, define

$$
\begin{aligned}
S_{n,j,M}=\bigl\{(\theta,\eta)\in\Theta_n\times H_n:
&2^{j-1}\delta_n<d_\eta(\theta,\theta_0)\leq2^j\delta_n,\\
&d(\eta,\eta_0)\leq2^{-M}d_\eta(\theta,\theta_0)
\bigr\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

On the event

$$
d_{\widehat\eta_n}(\widehat\theta_n,\theta_0)
\geq2^M\{\delta_n+d(\widehat\eta_n,\eta_0)\},
$$

the pair $(\widehat\theta_n,\widehat\eta_n)$ belongs to one of the sets $S_{n,j,M}$ with $j\geq M$. Near maximization then implies

$$
\sup_{(\theta,\eta)\in S_{n,j,M}}
\mathbb P_n(m_{\theta,\eta}-m_{\theta_0,\eta})\geq0.
$$

For $(\theta,\eta)\in S_{n,j,M}$, (5.55a) and the nuisance restriction give, for sufficiently large $M$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(m_{\theta,\eta}-m_{\theta_0,\eta})+e_n(\theta,\eta)
&\leq-(1-2^{-2M})d_\eta^2(\theta,\theta_0)\\
&\leq-2^{2j-4}\delta_n^2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore a nonnegative empirical criterion difference requires

$$
\sup_{(\theta,\eta)\in S_{n,j,M}}
\left|
\mathbb G_n(m_{\theta,\eta}-m_{\theta_0,\eta})
-\sqrt n e_n(\theta,\eta)
\right|
\geq
\sqrt n\,2^{2j-4}\delta_n^2.
$$

By Markov's inequality, (5.55b), and the monotonicity of $\phi_n(\delta)/\delta^\beta$, this event has outer probability at most

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\phi_n(2^j\delta_n)}
{\sqrt n\,2^{2j-4}\delta_n^2}
&\leq
C\frac{2^{j\beta}\phi_n(\delta_n)}
{\sqrt n\,2^{2j}\delta_n^2}\\
&\leq C2^{-j(2-\beta)}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\beta<2$,

$$
\sum_{j\geq M}C2^{-j(2-\beta)}\longrightarrow0
\qquad\text{as }M\to\infty.
$$

This proves

$$
d_{\widehat\eta_n}(\widehat\theta_n,\theta_0)
=O_P^*\{\delta_n+d(\widehat\eta_n,\eta_0)\}
$$

for exact maximizers. If the criterion is maximized only up to $O_P(\delta_n^2)$, restrict first to an event on which the tolerance is at most $K\delta_n^2$. Increasing $M$ makes the quadratic drift on every shell dominate this fixed multiple, after which the same geometric-series bound applies. Finally let $K$ increase. This proves the stated version.

</details>

::: {.callout-tip title="Chapter 25 destination"}

The theorem isolates two sources of target error:

$$
\text{intrinsic criterion rate }\delta_n
\quad+\quad
\text{nuisance discrepancy }d(\widehat\eta_n,\eta_0).
$$

[Theorem 25.81](chapter-25.qmd#theorem-25-81) returns to this balance for approximately least-favorable likelihoods. In current-status problems, an empirical-process modulus yields a cube-root nuisance rate; in partially linear and DML-style problems, orthogonality changes the relevant remainder from a first-order nuisance error to a product or quadratic error.

:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Chapter takeaway"}

The route is now complete:

1. uniform convergence plus identification gives consistency;
2. stochastic equicontinuity and a population derivative give a Z-estimator expansion;
3. estimating a nuisance adds a population drift that must be controlled;
4. one Newton correction recovers the same first-order law as a full root;
5. rate theorems balance deterministic curvature against empirical fluctuation, with nuisance error added explicitly.

Chapter 25 changes the objects being estimated, but not this architecture.

:::
